items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "hypothesis".

items.stem: Compare a hypothesis with a null hypothesis.
items.answer: A hypothesis predicts a specific relationship or difference based on reasoning; a null hypothesis states that there is no significant difference or relationship and is what the statistical test evaluates.

items.stem: Explain why a research question should be focused rather than broad.

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "Graphs are more useful than statistical tests in communicating environmental data."
items.answer: Graphs and statistics are complementary: graphs communicate patterns and tests confirm whether they are significant.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: show patterns and anomalies clearly; accessible to non-specialists. Limitations / counter-points: can mislead through scale choices; do not show whether differences are significant. Conclusion: Graphs and statistics are complementary: graphs communicate patterns and tests confirm whether they are significant. items.answer: systematic sampling
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of systematic sampling.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "null hypothesis"?
options: A statistical test of association between categorical variables, comparing observed with expected frequencies
A weakness in the method or data that reduces the validity or reliability of the conclusion
A statistical test comparing the means of two samples to determine whether they differ significantly
A statement that there is no significant difference or relationship between variables, used in statistical testing
items.answer: A statement that there is no significant difference or relationship between variables, used in statistical testing
items.markingKey: D. "null hypothesis" is a statement that there is no significant difference or relationship between variables, used in statistical testing.

items.stem: State two differences between validity and reliability.
items.answer: Validity is whether the method measures what it is intended to and answers the RQ; reliability is whether repeated measurements give consistent results.

items.stem: Explain why a pilot study is useful.
items.answer: It tests whether methods work, reveals practical problems, helps determine suitable quadrat size, sample number and range of the IV, and checks that questionnaire questions are clear.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It tests whether methods work, reveals practical problems, helps determine suitable quadrat size, sample number and range of the IV, and checks that questionnaire questions are clear. items.stem: Compare a t-test with a chi-squared test.
items.answer: A t-test compares the means of two samples of continuous data; a chi-squared test assesses association between categorical variables using frequency counts.
items.markingKey: A t-test compares the means of two samples of continuous data; a chi-squared test assesses association between categorical variables using frequency counts. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: Tomás writes: "A good research question can be answered with a simple yes or no." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Good RQs ask about the effect, relationship or extent ("What is the effect of…", "To what extent…") so that quantitative analysis is possible.
items.markingKey: Good RQs ask about the effect, relationship or extent ("What is the effect of…", "To what extent…") so that quantitative analysis is possible. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline why random sampling reduces bias.
items.answer: Each location has an equal chance of selection, so the investigator cannot consciously or unconsciously choose sites that support the hypothesis; the sample is more likely to be representative.
items.markingKey: Each location has an equal chance of selection, so the investigator cannot consciously or unconsciously choose sites that support the hypothesis; the sample is more likely to be representative. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Give one strength and one limitation of the claim that citizen science data are reliable enough to be used in environmental research.
items.answer: With standardised protocols and validation, citizen science data are valuable for detecting large-scale trends, though less reliable for fine detail.

items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that statistical tests are essential for drawing valid conclusions in environmental investigations.
items.answer: Statistical tests strengthen quantitative conclusions, but they must suit the data and be interpreted with ecological and social context.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: distinguish real patterns from chance; quantify confidence; objective decision rule. Limitations / counter-points: small samples give low power; tests depend on assumptions; qualitative data may be more appropriate for social studies; significance is not importance. Conclusion: Statistical tests strengthen quantitative conclusions, but they must suit the data and be interpreted with ecological and social context.
